contentBlocks.text: Welcome to Statistics & Data Science. Every real statistical investigation, from a simple class survey to a major scientific study, follows the same four-step cycle.

The statistical inquiry cycle has four steps: (1) Formulate a question — one that anticipates variability and can actually be answered with data, (2) Collect data — gathering it in a way appropriate to the question, (3) Analyze the data — using appropriate numerical and graphical methods, (4) Interpret the results — connecting the analysis back to the original question, including its limitations. These steps aren't optional extras — skipping any one of them weakens the whole investigation. For example: 'How many books do students in this class read per month?' is a real statistical question (it anticipates variation between students), while 'Do students like reading?' is too vague to collect clean data for. Take a topic you're curious about and write one genuine statistical question about it — one that anticipates real variability and could be answered with actual data.
This four-step cycle is the framework for everything in this course. Tomorrow we'll look closely at step two: how you actually collect data well.

objectives: Identify the four steps of the statistical inquiry cycle: formulate, collect, analyze, interpret
Write a genuine statistical question that anticipates variability and can be answered with data
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Introduce the four-step inquiry cycle with the books-read-per-month example.
2. Discuss the difference between a genuine statistical question and a vague one.
3. Have the child write their own statistical question on a topic of interest.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's topic: data collection.
differentiationTips: Struggling: provide 2-3 example question pairs (one statistical, one too vague) to sort before writing their own
Ready for more: ask them to explain why 'anticipating variability' is a necessary quality of a genuine statistical question, not just a nice-to-have
This is the first lesson of the course — a good moment to frame the whole year around this repeating four-step cycle
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. The four steps are: formulate a question, collect data, analyze data, interpret results. 2. A genuine statistical question anticipates real variability in the answer and can actually be answered by collecting data — 'How many books do students read per month?' works; 'Do students like reading?' is too vague.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses the course's data-science inquiry cycle description, establishing the GAISE-based four-step framework (formulate, collect, analyze, interpret) that WA's 2026 standards weave through statistics instruction.
